title: How To Handle Students Who Tattle, Complain, And Need Your Frequent Attention n-and-need-your-frequent-attention/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a three-step strategy for handling students who chronically interrupt with complaints or tattling: Enforce, Listen, and Fix. First, teachers must consistently enforce the hand-raising routine and never respond to students who bypass it, since responding to interruptions only worsens them. Second, once there's a natural break, teachers should give full, validating attention to the student's concern, however trivial it may seem. Third, teachers should address the issue quickly and assertively, whether the concern is valid or not, using sample scripted language for both cases. He argues that taking students' concerns seriously—paradoxically—is what curbs the frequency and intensity of tattling, because it frees students from anxiety and lets them refocus on academic work.
points: Step 1 (Enforce): never respond to or call on students who bypass the hand-raising routine, even when they wave or make noise for attention.
Step 2 (Listen): only address concerns during a natural break, giving full eye contact and attention regardless of how trivial the issue seems.
Step 3 (Fix): respond quickly and assertively to the concern, whether validating it or gently redirecting an unfounded complaint.
Taking students' concerns seriously—rather than waving them off—is what actually reduces future interruptions and tattling.
When students trust the teacher will safeguard their right to learn without interference, they let go of vigilance and refocus on academics.
quotes: The student is one of several who frequently need your attention—to tell on a classmate, voice a complaint, or ask why he gets to do this or she gets to do that.
But in the long run, an exasperated response will only cause their complaining and tattling to worsen.
Effective teaching requires you to never let the whole of your class suffer because of a small few.
By showing that you care, by validating their concerns and perturbations, your students will be free to let them go, focus on their academic responsibilities.
It may seem counterintuitive, but the best way to curb the intensity and frequency of tattling is to take it seriously.
But when they know they can count on you to safeguard their right to learn and enjoy school without interference, they’ll lay down their sword.
